column1: Give the three-part definition of a stakeholder.
column2: Someone who can be affected by the project, can impact the project, or can influence the project - in each case positively or negatively.

column1: Why does the definition say "real or perceived"?
column2: Because a stakeholder who believes they are affected is a stakeholder - perception alone generates power, opposition and requirements.

column1: What five things do stakeholders differ on?
column2: Roles, interests, influences, impacts and needs.

column1: How does "the government" as a stakeholder change from ENGGEN303 to 403?
column2: It decomposes - central government into individual ministries, local government into individual councils, and further down again.

column1: Recite the five steps of stakeholder analysis.
column2: Identify all stakeholders; investigate motivation factors; assess their power/influence and interest; determine requirements; develop critical success factors.

column1: What is step 2, investigating motivation factors, actually used to decide?
column2: Whether a stakeholder group needs to be broken down further.

column1: Roughly how many critical success factors should you end with?
column2: About six.

column1: What three things combine to produce wickedness?
column2: Complexity, uncertainty and value divergence.

column1: What question does the complexity circle answer?
column2: How complex is the problem?

column1: What question does the uncertainty circle answer?
column2: How much do we know - do we understand why it is occurring or how to address it?

column1: What question does the value divergence circle answer?
column2: How far apart are the stakeholders' values?

column1: What is the relationship between problem complexity and value divergence?
column2: The more complex the problem, the more value divergence you will deal with.

column1: Name the eight stakeholder attributes from Bryson.
column2: Power/influence, interest, position/attitude, urgency, responsibility, accountability, consulted, informed.

column1: Who wrote "What to do when stakeholders matter"?
column2: John M Bryson, 2004.

column1: Name the four directions used to generate a stakeholder list.
column2: Upwards, downwards, outwards, sidewards.

column1: Who sits in the "upwards" direction?
column2: Governments.

column1: Who sits in the "downwards" direction?
column2: Everyday people.

column1: Who sits in the "outwards" direction?
column2: Businesses you might consult with.

column1: Who sits in the "sidewards" direction?
column2: Other countries you can look at for reference.

column1: What two further splits apply to the stakeholder list?
column2: Direct versus indirect, and positive versus negative.

column1: Define power or influence in the power-interest matrix.
column2: The ability to change or stop a project.

column1: Define interest in the power-interest matrix.
column2: The size of the overlap between the stakeholder's goals and the project's goals.

column1: What is unusual about the lecture's definition of interest?
column2: It is goal overlap, not how much the stakeholder cares.

column1: Name the four quadrants of the power-interest matrix.
column2: Manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, and monitor.

column1: What two axes does the project frames grid use?
column2: Power/influence, and support and opposition.

column1: What does the support and opposition axis measure?
column2: Whether stakeholders agree or do not agree with the project - or with the problem.

column1: Why does "or the problem" matter in the support/opposition axis?
column2: A stakeholder may accept your solution while denying that there is a problem at all.

column1: Why plot stakeholders on multiple grids?
column2: Because support and power are independent - someone can be a strong supporter with far less power than assumed.

column1: What three axes does the stakeholder cube use?
column2: Power, interest and attitude.

column1: What does attitude mean in the stakeholder cube?
column2: Whether a stakeholder will back or block the project.

column1: What is the stated weakness of the stakeholder cube?
column2: It is difficult to see relationships between stakeholders, and difficult to see how positions change over time.

column1: What is a cross-section of the stakeholder cube?
column2: The power-interest matrix - the third axis is attitude.

column1: Name the three attributes in the salience model.
column2: Power, legitimacy and urgency.

column1: Define power in the salience model.
column2: The authority to change the project.

column1: Define legitimacy in the salience model.
column2: That the stakeholder's involvement is appropriate.

column1: Define urgency in the salience model.
column2: That the stakeholder's need requires immediate attention - it is time-sensitive and has criticality.

column1: Which salience category holds power only?
column2: Dormant.

column1: Which salience category holds legitimacy only?
column2: Discretionary.

column1: Which salience category holds urgency only?
column2: Demanding.

column1: Which salience category holds power and legitimacy?
column2: Dominant.

column1: Which salience category holds power and urgency?
column2: Dangerous.

column1: Which salience category holds legitimacy and urgency?
column2: Dependent.

column1: Which salience category holds all three attributes?
column2: Definitive.

column1: What is a stakeholder with none of the three attributes?
column2: A non-stakeholder - dropped from the analysis.

column1: Which salience categories map to "manage closely"?
column2: Definitive.

column1: Which salience categories map to "keep satisfied"?
column2: Dominant and dangerous.

column1: Which salience category maps to "keep informed"?
column2: Dependent.

column1: Which salience categories map to "monitor"?
column2: Dormant, discretionary and demanding.

column1: What practical job does legitimacy do in the salience model?
column2: It gives you a defensible way to eliminate stakeholders from the analysis.

column1: Why is the salience model called dynamic?
column2: Because urgency is time-sensitive - re-running the map over a two-year versus five-year horizon moves stakeholders between categories.

column1: What does RACI stand for in this lecture?
column2: Responsible, Accountable, Contributor, Informed.

column1: Define Responsible in the RACI framework.
column2: Stakeholders responsible for action and implementation.

column1: Define Accountable in the RACI framework.
column2: Stakeholders responsible for making key decisions.

column1: Define Contributor in the RACI framework.
column2: Stakeholders who provide input to make the answer better.

column1: Define Informed in the RACI framework.
column2: Stakeholders who need to know about decisions.

column1: What is unusual about the C in this version of RACI?
column2: It is Contributor, not the more common Consulted.

column1: What is the structural rule of RACI?
column2: A stakeholder can fall into only one grouping, though a grouping can hold multiple stakeholders.

column1: In the energy infrastructure RACI example, who is accountable and why?
column2: Iwi and landowners - the project needs new land, so they hold the power to say yes.

column1: In the energy infrastructure RACI example, who is responsible?
column2: The energy companies.

column1: In the energy infrastructure RACI example, what role does the Minister of Energy hold?
column2: Contributor.

column1: What does the energy RACI example show that a power-interest grid can miss?
column2: Who actually holds the veto.

column1: What are the six questions asked of each key stakeholder?
column2: What is their role, what is important to them, what is their attitude, what shifts do we need, how can they use their power, and how do they relate.

column1: What makes a stakeholder a "key" stakeholder?
column2: They repeatedly have large impacts on the project across multiple models.

column1: Name the three requirement tiers.
column2: Necessary, nice to have, and aspirational.

column1: What is the test for a necessary requirement?
column2: The project cannot continue if it is not met.

column1: What is a nice-to-have requirement?
column2: Something stakeholders want that would help, but that might not be able to be met.

column1: What is an aspirational requirement?
column2: A stakeholder goal that realistically cannot be met in this timeframe - record it, but do not address it.

column1: What is the classic error when sorting requirements?
column2: Sorting necessary and nice-to-have together.

column1: How would requirements be gathered in industry?
column2: Interviews and surveys with each stakeholder group.

column1: What are Systems Week teams told to use instead of interviews?
column2: Discussion with teammates, and AI to generate stakeholder positions provided it cites back to primary source material.

column1: Name three analytical techniques for mapping stakeholder relationships.
column2: Actor-linkage matrices, social network analysis, and knowledge mapping.

column1: What three things does social network analysis look at?
column2: Communication, trust and influence.

column1: What is the first thing to do with conflicting requirements?
column2: Classify the conflict - is it tractable or intractable, and what kind of conflict is it.

column1: What are the three moves for resolving conflicting requirements?
column2: Brainstorm with representatives to reach agreement; look for a compromise, including reclassifying whether the requirement is really necessary; and look for another way to meet the requirement.

column1: What three things must the final requirement list contain?
column2: The need-to-haves, the conflicts explicitly addressed, and buy-in from the key stakeholders.

column1: Which reading underpins the conflicting-requirements slide?
column2: Head, 2008, "Wicked Problems in Public Policy".

column1: Define a critical success factor.
column2: A requirement that potential solutions are assessed against.

column1: How do you find critical success factors?
column2: By looking at overlaps of necessary requirements recurring across stakeholders.

column1: State the relationship between CSFs and necessary requirements.
column2: All CSFs are necessary requirements, but not all necessary requirements are CSFs.

column1: What increases the number of CSFs you may need?
column2: A more complex problem, or more problem spaces.

column1: How many CSFs have some past projects had, and what is the target?
column2: Some have had 10 to 15; the target for Systems Week and the Team Project is closer to six.

column1: What is the named failure mode when selecting CSFs?
column2: Over-specification - assessing against 30 necessary requirements and losing sight of the overall problem.

column1: How many key stakeholders did the plastics team identify?
column2: Twelve, all showing power, legitimacy and urgency.

column1: Why did the plastics team exclude consumer businesses and households?
column2: They had a legitimate claim but the lowest power and interest, so they were not important enough to use in the analysis.

column1: What does the plastics case show about legitimacy alone?
column2: Legitimacy stops you being a non-stakeholder, but it does not earn a place in the CSFs.

column1: Where does commercial fishing sit on the consensus quadrant?
column2: Bottom left - low scientific consensus and low values consensus, the worst quadrant.

column1: Why does commercial fishing "hit gold" on wickedness?
column2: It is maximally complex, maximally uncertain, and has extreme value divergence.

column1: Name the four parts of the commercial fishing system boundary problem.
column2: Inshore fisheries, deep sea within the exclusive economic zone, high seas with no jurisdiction at all, and impacts from land.

column1: Why can't fishing boundaries be drawn cleanly?
column2: Fish swim, so they do not notice the boundary between inshore, deep sea and high sea.

column1: What was the fisheries team's catchphrase about knowledge?
column2: It's dark down there.

column1: What do people do with data in a contested space like fisheries?
column2: They cling to small data sets and call them true and applicable for the whole ocean.

column1: What happened when the word "abundant" was used in a stakeholder room?
column2: Half the room folded their arms and asked whose side you were on - you were speaking abundance language.

column1: Why are fisheries stakeholders suspicious of technology?
column2: Any technology that makes it easier to find fish makes it easier to catch fish, depleting stocks further.

column1: What was in scope for the commercial fishing report?
column2: Commercial fisheries only.

column1: What was out of scope for the commercial fishing report?
column2: Quota ownership and Crown obligations, aquaculture, recreational fishing including catch reporting, customary non-commercial fishing, and marine protection areas.

column1: What is the one-line problem with the fisheries scope?
column2: Out of scope were all the things the stakeholders felt strongly about.

column1: Why did the treaty settlement widen the range of Maori views?
column2: It awarded commercial rights to some iwi but not others, so some were firmly commercial while others had no commercial interest and set themselves up as kaitiaki of the ocean.

column1: Why were commercial fishers angry about recreational fishing being out of scope?
column2: Because it includes chartered operations where people pay to go out and catch a lot of fish at once.

column1: What did environmental lobbies and academia think the fisheries project should have been about?
column2: Marine protection areas - where you can and cannot fish, rather than how you fish.

column1: What is the one-line lesson of the fisheries boundary problem?
column2: Looking at one system, in a system of systems, is fraught.

column1: Which salience category did the fisheries stakeholders cluster in?
column2: Dangerous - power and urgency, with a vested interest in derailing the project.

column1: Which agencies had to be engaged on commercial fishing?
column2: Fisheries NZ within MPI, the Ministry for the Environment, DOC, MBIE, LINZ, regional councils, Customs, MFAT, Maritime NZ and the EPA.

column1: What was the point of showing the ten-agency government map?
column2: Not to memorise the agencies, but to remember that the stakeholder map within government is likely to be very complex.

column1: How did panel selection go wrong in practice?
column2: Experts had to be excluded because they could not function in the same room, which undermined the legitimacy of the process.

column1: What happened in the fisheries project's shared Google Doc?
column2: People fought in it, so all feedback had to be taken separately.

column1: Why were recommendations withheld during consultation?
column2: Because stakeholders got so hung up on their vested interests - they saw the text but not the recommendations.

column1: What did the fisheries panel decide their critical success factor was?
column2: Broadening the scope.

column1: What did the panel do about the scope problem?
column2: They went back and renegotiated their terms of reference with the Prime Minister.

column1: Why were themes 1 to 3 included when they were not asked for?
column2: To provide context that made the stakeholders feel heard.

column1: Name themes 1 to 3 of the fisheries report.
column2: Strengthened leadership; a bold Oceans Strategic Action Plan; and Te ao Maori, a connected worldview in 2040 and beyond.

column1: What was the key leverage point produced by the fisheries report?
column2: A new portfolio - the Minister of Oceans and Fisheries - giving one person jurisdiction over every agency guarding the ocean.

column1: Was the Minister of Oceans and Fisheries recommendation science advice?
column2: No - it was an institutional change, and the highest-leverage recommendation in the report.

column1: What does theme 4 of the fisheries report call for?
column2: A refined set of regulatory tools, requiring Fisheries NZ, DOC and MfE to collaborate across agencies and Acts.

column1: What does theme 5 of the fisheries report call for?
column2: A data platform enabling informed commercial and environmental decision making - because we know frighteningly little and need to aggregate what we do know in compatible formats.

column1: What does theme 6 of the fisheries report call for?
column2: That the ecosystem approach to fisheries management be embraced within the current regulatory framework, including the Fisheries Act 1996.

column1: What was notable about EAFM and the Fisheries Act?
column2: It was already in the Act and nobody was using it - the Minister was already empowered to act.

column1: Which unused section of the Fisheries Act could protect ecosystems?
column2: Section 9c - habitats of particular significance to fisheries management.

column1: What does theme 7 of the fisheries report call for?
column2: Maximising research and innovation - innovation can only support oceans if the settings are right, but then there is enormous potential to fish smarter.

column1: What is precision seafood harvesting?
column2: A modified trawl net invented at Plant and Food that tricks fish into the net, lets small ones escape through holes, and holds the catch in a comfortable shoal environment instead of dragging the ocean floor.

column1: What does theme 8 of the fisheries report emphasise?
column2: That there is no one-size-fits-all approach - local knowledge and matauranga Maori are vital for place-based action, cumulative effects are crucial, and regional capability needs building.

column1: What is the soft limit in fisheries management?
column2: An agreed stock population level, set by Fisheries NZ but not agreed by everybody, at half of which quotas are reduced so the fishery can rebuild.

column1: What is the hard limit in fisheries management?
column2: The point at which the fish are gone and fishing must stop entirely, hoping the stock rebuilds - which internationally it sometimes never does.

column1: Why can fisheries numbers back up any argument?
column2: Because you do not know the unfished stock volume, you do not really know the sustainable volume, and you do not really know how many fish there are - three unknowns in one equation.

column1: What two things did all the fisheries stakeholders have in common?
column2: They were all really grumpy, and they all really cared about the ocean - putting them all in the urgent category.

column1: What happened to the fisheries recommendations initially?
column2: The opposition was briefed, a formal government response was arranged in eight themes, most were agreed or agreed with intent, and the recommendations fed into the Fisheries Industry Transformation Plan.

column1: What survived the change of government?
column2: The Minister of Oceans and Fisheries portfolio.

column1: What did not survive the change of government?
column2: Industry transformation plans were removed as a policy tool, so the fisheries plan was lost.

column1: What lesson does Juliet draw from concentrating power in one portfolio?
column2: That the power will be used differently depending on who is democratically elected - it is leverage that cuts both ways.

column1: What is the closing warning about boundaries?
column2: Every time you draw a boundary, you can create conflict - so the process must be iterative.

column1: What sometimes has to happen to get stakeholder buy-in?
column2: You have to broaden your scope or be flexible with your project plan.

column1: Who delivered ENGGEN403 Lecture 7?
column2: Amanda Di Ienno and Juliet Gerrard.
